title: Lāmiyyat al-afʿāl
author: Ibn Mālik
subject: sarf
summary: Lāmiyyat al-afʿāl, Ibn Mālik's poem on the verb, has 114 verses in the basīṭ metre, every one rhyming in lām (hence its name). It is the ṣarf poem of the Maghrib and of al-Azhar, learnt by heart and read with a commentary, among them that of the poet's son Badr al-Dīn. In a few lines each it sets out the patterns of the bare and augmented verb and the vowel of the muḍāriʿ, the muḍāriʿ, the passive and the command, the participles, the maṣdars, the nouns of time and place, the land of abundance and the instrument, packing long lists of verbs and nouns into its verses. The lessons give the verses as the Cairo print of 1896 has them, vowelled after the metre, explain each rule with examples from the verses, from the Ottoman ṣarf books and from The Nahwi's conjugation tool, and say where the print is doubtful.

lessons.title: The opening: whoever masters the verb
body: Lāmiyyat al-afʿāl is a poem by Ibn Mālik (d. 672/1274), the author of the Alfiyya, on the forms of the verb and the nouns made from it. It has 114 verses in the metre called basīṭ, and every verse ends in the same rhyme, lām with a long a: badalā, al-amalā, al-fuḍalā. A poem rhyming in lām is a lāmiyya; this is “the lāmiyya of the verbs”.

It opens as such poems do: with praise of God, “I seek no substitute for it”, and blessing upon “the best of creatures”, the Prophet, his family and his companions. Then, after wa-baʿdu, the theme: “the verb: whoever masters its conjugation gains of the language its chapters and its ways”. The verb is the hub of ṣarf: the participles, the maṣdars and the nouns of place and instrument that fill the second half of the poem are all taken from it.

The second line of the opening states the method of every teaching poem (naẓm): “take a poem that takes in what matters; and he may grasp the details who keeps the summaries in mind”. The verses are short summaries, to be learnt by heart; the details are unfolded by a teacher or a commentary. The Lāmiyya is so compressed that it is almost always read with one, and the lessons here do the same work: each takes a few verses and opens them up.

Some habits of verse to know before reading on. A word may be split between the two halves of a line (we write the halves with “ * ” between them). A hamza is sometimes dropped for the metre, its vowel given to the letter before it (aw and ayḍan are then written with a bare alif). A pattern is often named by an example verb rather than by its name, and lists of verbs are given with a word of meaning (“that is …”) so that the right sense is meant.

Our text is the Cairo print of 1896, a collection of the much-used mutūn; it has almost no vowels, so the vowels are ours, fixed by the metre and, from verse 62 on and at doubtful places, by W. Volck's edition of 1866 with the commentary of Ibn Mālik's son Badr al-Dīn.

lessons.title: The four bare patterns, and the muḍāriʿ of faʿula and faʿila
body: The bare verb, Ibn Mālik begins, comes on faʿlala, on faʿula, “with a kasra on the ʿayn” (faʿila), or on faʿala. The four-letter pattern comes first, then the three pasts of the triliteral, told apart only by the vowel of the ʿayn. Daḥraja yudaḥriju is the model of faʿlala, as the Ottoman books recite it.

Then the muḍāriʿ. “Keep the ḍamma of faʿula in the muḍāriʿ”: karuma yakrumu, u in both. “And give a fatḥa to the place of the kasra in what is built from faʿila”: ʿalima yaʿlamu, the kasra of the past turned into a fatḥa. These two are rules without exceptions for faʿula, and with exceptions for faʿila, which follow at once.

“Two ways are in it” in a group of faʿila verbs, whose muḍāriʿ may take a fatḥa or a kasra: ḥasiba (named by its command iḥsib), waghira, ḥāra, naʿima (inʿim), baʾisa, yaʾisa, waliha (iwlah), yabisa and wahila. With the conjugation tool: yaḥsabu and yaḥsibu, yanʿamu and yanʿimu.

“And keep the kasra alone” in another group: waritha, waliya, warima, wariʿa, wamiqa, wafiqa, wathiqa and wariya al-mukhkhu, “the marrow was full”. These are faʿila yafʿilu, the rare bāb of ḥasiba. Look at them: every one begins with a wāw. They are mithāl verbs, and their wāw drops in the future before the kasra (yarithu, yamiqu), as the Marāḥ explains; the Marāḥ names wamiqa yamiqu as one of the mithāl's bābs.

Notice how the verse names the verbs: some by the past with -ta (waghirta, ḥirta, baʾista), some by the command (iḥsib, inʿim, iwlah), some by the bare past (yabis, wahilā). The form is chosen for the metre; what is meant each time is the verb and its root.

lessons.title: The muḍāriʿ of faʿala: weak letters and the doubled verb
body: Faʿala, the commonest past, can take any of the three vowels in its muḍāriʿ, and the poem now says what decides. “Keep a kasra for the ʿayn of the muḍāriʿ that follows faʿala” in four kinds: with a wāw as its fāʾ (waʿada yaʿidu), with a yāʾ as its ʿayn (bāʿa yabīʿu), “like atā”, with a yāʾ as its lām (ramā yarmī), and the doubled verb “when intransitive”, as ḥanna ṭalā, “a young one yearned”.

“And give a ḍamma to the ʿayn of its transitive”: the doubled verb that takes an object has yafʿulu. The Marāḥ's examples show the pair: sarra yasurru, “to gladden” (someone), and farra yafirru, “to flee”, which takes no object. A doubled verb's muḍāriʿ is thus told by its transitivity.

Both rules have rare exceptions: “one with kasra is rare”, a transitive with yafʿilu; “as an intransitive with ḍamma has been allowed”. The first is ḥabbahu, “he loved him”, with yafʿilu. Some have “two ways”: harra, “he loathed”, shadda, “he bound”, and ʿallahu ʿalalan, “he gave him a second drink”, and batta, “he cut”. The intransitives with ḍamma are the long list of the next lesson.

Why do weak letters decide? A wāw as fāʾ drops before the kasra of yafʿilu (yaʿidu), and that kasra is what the mithāl is known by; a yāʾ as ʿayn or lām keeps its yāʾ only after a kasra (yabīʿu, yarmī), where a ḍamma would turn it into a wāw. So the vowel of the muḍāriʿ is not chosen freely: the root's weak letters pull it.

Keep the first half of the picture: faʿala takes yafʿilu with a wāw fāʾ, a yāʾ ʿayn, a yāʾ lām, or doubling without an object; yafʿulu with doubling and an object. The rest of faʿala is the subject of lessons 5 and 6.

lessons.title: Doubled verbs that break the rule
body: Three verses list the intransitive doubled verbs that take a ḍamma against the rule (yafʿulu, not yafʿilu), and then the verbs with both vowels. The first half-line, “give a ḍamma to namma … together with intransitivity”, does not scan in our print, and Volck's edition reads it otherwise; we give it as printed. The list it opens is clear: umrur bihi, “pass by him”, jalla “like jalā”, “he emigrated”, habbat, “the wind blew”, dharrat, “the sun rose”, ajja, “the fire blazed”, karra, “he turned back to attack”, hamma bihi, “he set his mind on it”, ʿamma, zamma, saḥḥa, “it poured”, and more.

Some entries carry a gloss with ay, “that is”: malla ay dhamalā, “he went at a brisk pace”; shadda ay ʿadā, “he ran”; ghalla ay dakhalā, “he entered”; thalla ay rātha. The gloss matters, because the same verb in another sense follows the rule: shadda “he bound”, transitive, was among the two-way verbs of verse 12; shadda “he ran”, intransitive, takes the ḍamma here. The list continues with qashsha, janna, “the night covered him”, rashsha and ṭashsha, “the cloud sprinkled, drizzled”, ṭalla, “blood went unavenged”, khabba, “the horse trotted”, kamma and ʿassat, “the she-camel was stingy with her milk”.

Then “take the two ways” of ṣadda, “he turned away”, atta (the print's reading; Volck has aththa), kharra, “the rock fell with a noise”, ḥaddat, “she mourned”, tharrat and darrat, “the udder, the milk flowed”, jadda, jamma, shabba, “the horse reared”, ʿanna, “it appeared”, faḥḥat, “the snake hissed”, and, in the next verse, shaṭṭat al-dāru, nassa and ḥarra. Shaḥḥa ay bakhila, “he was stingy”, is marked as irregular. (Verse 15 is also uncertain: “ṣarkhan” in our print, “ṣawtan” in Volck.)

How is a student to use such lists? He learns them by heart as he learns the verse, and with them the meanings the glosses fix; the commentary gives each verb's muḍāriʿ. The rule stays simple, and the list holds its exceptions: the doubled verb takes yafʿulu if transitive and yafʿilu if intransitive, except the verbs named here.
The conjugation tool does not conjugate doubled verbs, and our print gives no futures for these, so the lesson names them by their pasts only.

lessons.title: Faʿala with a wāw, verbs of contest, and the throat letters
body: Now the ḍamma. “The muḍāriʿ of faʿaltu, if there is the wāw as its ʿayn or as its lām, is brought with a ḍamma on the ʿayn”: qāla yaqūlu, ghazā yaghzū. The reason mirrors that of the kasra: a wāw keeps its letter after a ḍamma, as a yāʾ does after a kasra.

“And this rule has been given to what indicates a contest in boasting”: the verb of outdoing, when you say that you vied with someone in a quality and beat him (the grammarians call it mughālaba). Its muḍāriʿ takes a ḍamma, whatever its usual bāb, provided it “has not what calls for the ʿayn to have a kasra necessarily”: a wāw as fāʾ, or a yāʾ as ʿayn or lām, keeps the kasra even here.

Then the fatḥa. “A fatḥa on [the ʿayn of the muḍāriʿ of] a verb that has a letter of the throat other than its first has been reported from al-Kisāʾī in this kind”: in the verbs of contest, he allowed the throat letter's fatḥa. “In other than this”, outside the contest, the verb whose ʿayn or lām is a throat letter takes a fatḥa “by agreement”, as yasʾalu from saʾala, and yaftaḥu from fataḥa.

“Other than its first”: a throat letter as fāʾ does not count (ʿatala, lesson 6). And the fatḥa is the rule only “if it is not doubled and not known for a kasra or a ḍamma”: baghā has a ghayn but is yabghī, and dakhala has a khāʾ but is yadkhulu, because usage has fixed them.

So for faʿala the poem gives an order of causes: a weak letter or doubling first, then the contest, then a throat letter, and over all of them usage. The next lesson gives what is left when none of these applies.

lessons.title: Kasra or ḍamma; and the hollow verb with -tu and -na
lessons.arabic: الْكَسْرُ أَوِ الضَّمُّ، وَنَقْلُ حَرَكَةِ الْعَيْنِ
lessons.transliteration: al-kasr aw al-ḍamm, wa-naql ḥarakat al-ʿayn
body: What remains of faʿala? “The ʿayn of the muḍāriʿ of faʿaltu, where it is free of anything that brings the fatḥa, as what is built from ʿatala, give it a kasra or a ḍamma, when the choosing of one of them has fallen away for lack of being well known or of a cause.” If usage has fixed a vowel, follow it; if a weak letter, doubling or a contest fixes it, follow that; if neither, both are right. ʿAtala, “to drag”, is the example: its throat letter is its first, which does not count, and so the conjugation tool gives both yaʿtilu and yaʿtulu.

So the poem's answer for faʿala in full: kasra with a wāw fāʾ, a yāʾ ʿayn or lām, or doubling without object; ḍamma with doubling with object, a wāw ʿayn or lām, or a contest; fatḥa with a throat letter as ʿayn or lām; and, failing all these and failing usage, kasra or ḍamma freely.

The next section, a single verse and a half, turns to the hollow verb with the pronouns -tu and -na. “Move to the fāʾ of the triliteral the vowel of the ʿayn when it is weak, and the verb is joined to the tāʾ of the pronoun or its nūn”: khawifna becomes khifna, the kasra of the wāw moving to the khāʾ; ṭawulna becomes ṭulna, its ḍamma moving to the ṭāʾ.

“And when it is a fatḥa, then in its place take a vowel of the kind of that ʿayn”: qawalna and bayaʿna have a fatḥa on the weak letter, which cannot be moved to a fāʾ that already has one; so the fāʾ takes the vowel that belongs with the weak letter, a ḍamma for the wāw, a kasra for the yāʾ: qulna, biʿna; qultu, biʿtu.

The Marāḥ gives the same rule with all its steps (its lesson on qulna and khifna); the Lāmiyya puts it in two half-lines. Compare the two: the reason is the same, that the vowel left on the first letter points to the weak letter that has gone.

tasks.prompt: When may the muḍāriʿ of faʿala take either kasra or ḍamma?
tasks.answer: When it has no throat letter as ʿayn or lām, no weak letter or doubling or contest that fixes a vowel, and usage has not fixed one; as ʿatala: yaʿtilu or yaʿtulu.

tasks.prompt: Summarise the poem's rules for the vowel of the muḍāriʿ of faʿala.
tasks.answer: Kasra: wāw as fāʾ, yāʾ as ʿayn or lām, doubled intransitive. Ḍamma: doubled transitive, wāw as ʿayn or lām, a verb of contest. Fatḥa: a throat letter as ʿayn or lām. Usage overrides; failing all, kasra or ḍamma.

tasks.prompt: Explain khifna and qulna by the rule of verses 27–28.
tasks.answer: Khawifna: the weak ʿayn has a kasra, which moves to the fāʾ: khifna. Qawalna: the ʿayn has a fatḥa, which cannot be moved to the fāʾ; so the fāʾ takes the vowel of the wāw's kind, a ḍamma: qulna.

parts.title: The augmented verb, the muḍāriʿ, the passive and the command

lessons.title: The augmented patterns, named by example
body: The chapter on the augmented verb lists its patterns by example, in a single run: “like aʿlama the verb comes with augmentation, with wālā, wallā, istaqāma, iḥranjama, infaṣala”. Read each verb as its pattern: aʿlama is afʿala, wālā fāʿala, wallā faʿʿala, istaqāma istafʿala, infaṣala infaʿala, iʿtadala iftaʿala; iḥranjama is ifʿanlala, a quadriliteral with two letters added.

Some patterns are named outright: “ifʿalla, with an alif in the middle as the fourth and without it”, that is ifʿālla and ifʿalla, as iḥmārra and iḥmarra in the Marāḥ. Others come as verbs: ihbayyakha, “he walked proudly”, is ifʿayyala; tadaḥrajat is tafaʿlala; iḥlawlā, “it was very sweet”, is ifʿawʿala; isbaṭarra, “he stretched out”, is ifʿalalla, like iqshaʿarra; tawallā and tawālā are tafaʿʿala and tafāʿala.

Many of the examples are attached forms (mulḥaq), triliteral roots made to look like four-letter verbs (see the Marāḥ's thirty-five bābs): jawrabat, “she put on socks”, is fawʿala; harwaltu, “I hurried”, faʿwala; qalnasat, “she put on a cap”, faʿnala; salqā, faʿlā; tamaskana, “he humbled himself”, tamafʿala; islanqā, “he lay on his back”, ifʿanlā; ittaṣala is iftaʿala with its wāw turned into tāʾ, as in ittaʿada.

The last three verses collect rarer patterns still (zahzaqtu, “I laughed heartily”, bayṭartu, “I worked as a farrier”, intakhala, “he sifted”, and many words that only a dictionary knows). Their vowels in our text are made from the patterns and have not yet been checked against Volck's edition, so learn them with your teacher; the lesson does not test them.

Ibn Mālik's point in listing so much is that each pattern is a class of verbs: to know iḥlawlā is to know how to read every ifʿawʿala. The conjugation tool gives the commonest of these patterns for sound roots.

وَاعْلَوَّطَ اعْثَوْجَجَتْ بَيْطَرْتُ سَنْبَلَ زَمْ * لَقَ اضْمُمَنْ لِتَسَلْقَى وَاجْتَنِبْ خَلَلَا
text.en:
zahzaqtu “I laughed heartily”, halqamtu “I gulped”, rahmastu “I spoke secretly”, ikwaʾalla “he was short”, tarahshafa / “he sipped”, ijfaʾaẓẓa “he was swollen”, islahamma “he changed colour”, qaṭrana al-jamalā “he smeared the camel with tar”,
tarmastu “I hid”, kaltabtu, jalmaṭtu “I shaved”, and wa-ghalṣama “and he cut the throat”, then / idlammasa “it was very dark”, ihrammaʿat “she hurried”, and wa-iʿlankasa “and it was thick”, intakhalā “he sifted”,
and wa-iʿlawwaṭa “and he clung to [the camel's] neck”, iʿthawjajat, bayṭartu “I tended [the beast] as a farrier”, sanbala “it put forth ears”, zamlaqa; / give the ḍamma for tasalqā, and avoid a defect.

lessons.title: The prefixes of the muḍāriʿ, and the vowel before the last
body: “Begin the muḍāriʿ with one of the letters of naʾtī”: nūn, hamza, tāʾ, yāʾ, the four prefixes the Marāḥ gathers in atayna. The prefix “has a ḍamma when it is joined to the quadriliteral, absolutely”: to any verb whose past has four letters, bare or augmented or attached, as yudaḥriju, yukrimu, yuqaṭṭiʿu, yuqātilu. “And give it a fatḥa when joined to other than it”: yaḍribu, yastakhriju, yatafaḍḍalu.

A dialect puts a kasra on the prefixes “other than the yāʾ” in three kinds: “the future of faʿila”, as tiʿlamu, niʿlamu; verbs beginning “with the hamza of joining”, as tistanṣiru; and verbs beginning with an added tāʾ, “as tazakkā”. The Marāḥ gives the same dialect, with its reason: the kasra recalls the kasra of the past (ʿalima, istanṣara).

“And it has been reported in the yāʾ” too, in verbs like abā, “he refused”, and in mithāl verbs with wāw like wajila, “he feared”. Our print's wording of this verse is doubtful (it does not scan, and Volck's edition reads it otherwise), so take from it only that the yāʾ is sometimes given the kasra in these verbs.

Then the vowel before the last letter, in the augmented verbs of this chapter. It is a kasra, necessarily, “if its past has been denied an added tāʾ at its beginning”: yukrimu, yuqaṭṭiʿu, yuqātilu, yanṣarifu, yastakhriju. If the past begins with an added tāʾ, “give a fatḥa to what is before the last”: yatafaḍḍalu, yataḍārabu, yatadaḥraju.

Two questions, then, decide the muḍāriʿ of any augmented verb: does the past have four letters (then the prefix takes a ḍamma)? And does it begin with a tāʾ (then the letter before the last takes a fatḥa)? The conjugation tool follows both rules.

tasks.prompt: Which prefixes take a ḍamma, and which a fatḥa?
tasks.answer: A ḍamma when the past has four letters, bare or augmented (yudaḥriju, yukrimu, yuqaṭṭiʿu, yuqātilu); a fatḥa in all other verbs (yaḍribu, yastakhriju, yatafaḍḍalu).

tasks.prompt: In which verbs does a dialect allow a kasra on the prefix, and on which prefixes?
tasks.answer: On the prefixes other than the yāʾ, in the future of faʿila (tiʿlamu), in verbs beginning with a hamza of joining (tistanṣiru), and in verbs beginning with an added tāʾ (like tazakkā).

tasks.answer: Yastakhriju, with a kasra before the last, because the past has no added tāʾ at its start; yataḍārabu, with a fatḥa, because its past begins with an added tāʾ.

text.en:
Begin the muḍāriʿ with one of [the letters of] naʾtī; and it has / a ḍamma when it is joined to the quadriliteral, absolutely,
and give it a fatḥa when joined to other than it; and for other / than the yāʾ allow a kasra in the future of faʿila,

text.original:
أَوْ مَا تَصَدَّرَ هَمْزُ الْوَصْلِ فِيهِ أَوِ التْ * تَا زَائِدًا كَتَزَكَّى، وَهْوَ قَدْ نُقِلَا
فِي الْيَا وَفِي غَيْرِهَا إِنْ أُلْحِقَ بِأَبَى * أَوْ مَا لَهُ الْوَاوُ فَاءٌ قَدْ وَجِلَا
text.en:
or [in] what begins with the hamza of joining, or [with] the tāʾ / as an added [letter], as tazakkā “he purified himself”; and it has been reported
in the yāʾ, and in other than it, if [the verb] is joined to abā “he refused”, / or [is] what has the wāw as its fāʾ, [as] wajilā “he feared”.

text.original:
وَكَسْرُ مَا قَبْلَ آخِرِ الْمُضَارِعِ مِنْ * ذَا الْبَابِ يَلْزَمُ إِنْ مَاضِيهِ قَدْ حُظِلَا
زِيَادَةَ التَّاءِ أَوَّلًا، وَإِنْ حَصَلَتْ * لَهُ فَمَا قَبْلَ الَاخِرِ افْتَحَنْ بِوَلَا
text.en:
A kasra on what is before the last [letter] of the muḍāriʿ of / this chapter is necessary, if its past has been denied
an added tāʾ at its beginning; and if [that] has come / to it, give a fatḥa to what is before the last, consistently.

lessons.title: The verb whose doer is not named
body: “If you attribute the verb to the object, bring it with a ḍamma on the first” letter: ḍuriba, yuḍrabu. “And give it a kasra when it is joined to a weak ʿayn”: in the hollow verb the first letter takes a kasra, qīla, bīʿa, the forms the Marāḥ derives from quwila and buyiʿa. “And put before the last, in the past, a kasra, and a fatḥa in what else follows”: ḍuriba and ukrima with kasra, yuḍrabu and yukramu with fatḥa.

Two kinds of verb need one more ḍamma. “The third letter of one with the hamza of joining: give it a ḍamma with it”, with the first: ustukhrija, uḥtuqira, the hamza and the tāʾ both with ḍamma. “And with the tāʾ of compliance (muṭāwaʿa) give a ḍamma to what follows it”: tufuḍḍila, tuḍūriba, the tāʾ and the letter after it. The tāʾ of tafaʿʿala and tafāʿala is called the tāʾ of compliance because these patterns often answer faʿʿala and fāʿala: the one who is acted on accepts the act.

Last, the hollow verbs with a hamza of joining. “What is given to the fāʾ of the like of bāʿa, give to the third of the like of ikhtāra and inqāda”: as bāʿa makes bīʿa, ikhtāra makes ikhtīra, “he was chosen”, and inqāda inqīda, “he was led”, the kasra on the third letter. The poem adds “which is the better”: the Marāḥ reports other dialects (with a touch of ḍamma, or with ū), and this one is preferred.

So the passive needs three things: a ḍamma at the start (or a kasra, in the hollow verb), the right vowel before the last (kasra in the past, fatḥa in the muḍāriʿ), and, in the long patterns, a second ḍamma on the letter the poem names. The conjugation tool gives the passive of every sound pattern that takes an object.

ثَالِثَ ذِي هَمْزِ وَصْلٍ ضُمَّ مَعْهُ، وَمَعْ * تَاءِ الْمُطَاوَعَةِ اضْمُمْ تِلْوَهَا بِوَلَا
وَمَا لِفَا نَحْوِ بَاعَ اجْعَلْ لِثَالِثِ نَحْ * وِ اخْتَارَ وَانْقَادَ كَاخْتِيرَ الَّذِي فَضَلَا
text.en:
The third [letter] of one with the hamza of joining: give it a ḍamma with it; and with / the tāʾ of compliance give a ḍamma to what follows it, consistently;
and what [is given] to the fāʾ of the like of bāʿa “he sold”, give to the third of the like / of ikhtāra “he chose” and inqāda “he submitted”, as ikhtīra “he was chosen”, which is the better.

lessons.title: The command
body: “From afʿala the command is afʿil”: akrim, “honour!”, with a hamza of cutting, the hamza of the pattern itself, which the Marāḥ shows dropped in tukrimu and back in the command. “And, for other than it, take it like the majzūm muḍāriʿ that has been cut off at its first”: the command is the jussive without its prefix. Tuqaṭṭiʿ gives qaṭṭiʿ, tuqātil gives qātil.

“And with a hamza of joining that has a kasra begin it, if it is an unvowelled letter that was joined to what was dropped”: taḍrib loses its tāʾ and leaves a quiescent ḍād, so iḍrib. “Give the hamza a ḍamma before a necessary ḍamma”: tanṣur gives unṣur, the ʿayn having a ḍamma that belongs to the form. Ughzī, “raid! (a woman)”, is the test: its zāy has a kasra, though its bāb has a ḍamma, so the ḍamma before which the hamza stands is not there; it is said “with a kasra touched with ḍamma”, and that “has been accepted”. Al-ʿIzzī, in the Ottoman print, writes it with a ḍamma.

Three verbs break the rule: mur, “command!”, khudh, “take!”, and kul, “eat!”, are irregular “with dropping”: from the roots ʾ-m-r, ʾ-kh-dh, ʾ-k-l, they drop their first hamza and need no hamza of joining. But after wa or fa, “wa-ʾmur has spread”, with the hamza kept, as in the Qurʾān's wa-ʾmur ahlaka bi-l-ṣalāti (20:132). The full forms of khudh and kul, with the hamza, are “rare”.

The rule in short: take the jussive, drop the prefix; if the first letter left is quiescent, add a hamza of joining, with a ḍamma if the ʿayn has a lasting ḍamma and otherwise a kasra; afʿala alone keeps its own hamza with a fatḥa.

مِنْ أَفْعَلَ الْأَمْرُ أَفْعِلْ، وَاعْزُهُ لِسِوَا * هُ كَالْمُضَارِعِ ذِي الْجَزْمِ الَّذِي اخْتُزِلَا
أَوَّلُهُ، وَبِهَمْزِ الْوَصْلِ مُنْكَسِرًا * صِلْ سَاكِنًا كَانَ بِالْمَحْذُوفِ مُتَّصِلَا
text.en:
From afʿala the command is afʿil; and, for other than it, take it / like the majzūm muḍāriʿ that has been cut off
at its first [letter]; and with a hamza of joining that has a kasra / begin [it] if it is an unvowelled [letter] that was joined to what was dropped.

وَالْهَمْزَ قَبْلَ لُزُومِ الضَّمِّ ضُمَّ، وَنَحْ * وَ اغْزِي بِكَسْرٍ مُشَمِّ الضَّمِّ قَدْ قُبِلَا
وَشَذَّ بِالْحَذْفِ مُرْ وَخُذْ وَكُلْ، وَفَشَا * وَأْمُرْ، وَمُسْتَنْدَرٌ تَتْمِيمُ خُذْ وَكُلَا
text.en:
Give the hamza a ḍamma before a necessary ḍamma; and the like / of ughzī “raid! (f.)” with a kasra touched with ḍamma has been accepted.
Irregular with dropping are mur “command!”, khudh “take!” and kul “eat!”, and wa-ʾmur “and command!” has spread; / and rare is giving khudh and kul their full form.

lessons.title: The active participle and the adjectives of the triliteral
body: “On the measure of fāʿil the active participle is made from the triliteral whose measure is not faʿula”: ḍārib from ḍaraba, ʿālim from ʿalima. Faʿula is left out: it is used, as the Marāḥ says, for natures and qualities, not acts, and its adjectives take other patterns.

“And from that”, from faʿula, “it is formed like sahl and al-ẓarīf”: faʿl and faʿīl, the two commonest, “easy”, “elegant”. Less often “afʿal, or faʿāl, or fuʿul”, and like al-furāt, “sweet water” (fuʿāl), ʿafr (faʿl), al-ḥaṣūr, “the chaste” (faʿūl), ghumr, “untried” (fuʿl), ʿāqir, “barren” (fāʿil), junub, “in a state of major impurity” (fuʿul), and what resembles thamil, “drunk” (faʿil). These are the patterns the Marāḥ calls “the adjective like the participle”.

“And from an intransitive on the measure faʿila it is formed on its own measure”: faʿil, as shaj, “grieved”, and like ʿajil, “hasty”; and also faʿl (al-shaʾz, “the rough”), afʿal (al-ashnab, “the one with fine white teeth”) and faʿlān (al-jazlān, “the glad”, as our print spells it; the usual word has a dhāl).

Then the poem allows a pattern to be borrowed from another class “by analogy with another, for a relation” of meaning: fānin, “perishing”, on fāʿil, and the singular of al-bukhalā, that is bakhīl, “miser”, on faʿīl; and, in forming from faʿula, khafīf, ṭayyib and ashyab. A word takes the pattern of the words it is like in sense.

The lesson for a reader: an adjective's pattern tells you something of its verb. Fāʿil points to an act (faʿala, faʿila transitive); faʿl, faʿīl and their sisters to a quality (faʿula); faʿil, afʿal and faʿlān to a state (faʿila intransitive). The next lesson adds that fāʿil can be made from any of them when an event is meant.

lessons.title: Fāʿil for the event; the participles of the longer verbs; mafʿūl
body: “Fāʿil serves for all, if what is meant is an event”: any triliteral, even one whose adjective is a ṣifa mushabbaha, may make fāʿil when you speak of a quality as a happening at a time. The example: ghadan dhā jādhilin, “tomorrow this one will be rejoicing”, from jadhila, whose usual adjective is jadhil, “glad”. Jādhil, on fāʿil, speaks of the joy that will come about tomorrow.

“With the active participle of what is not of three letters comes the measure of the muḍāriʿ, but at its beginning is put a mīm that takes a ḍamma”: yukrimu, mukrim; yastakhriju, mustakhrij. “And if what is before its last you give a fatḥa, it becomes a passive participle”: mukram, mustakhraj. The Marāḥ gives the same rule and its reasons.

From the triliteral the passive participle is “on the measure mafʿūl”: maḍrūb. “And what comes like faʿīl has been turned by it from the origin”: qatīl, jarīḥ, “killed, wounded”, stand for maqtūl, majrūḥ, but they are a departure from the rule, not a second rule.

“And they made do with the like of najan and al-nisy instead of the measure mafʿūl”: najan, “skin stripped off”, and nisy, “a forgotten thing”, carry a passive meaning without its pattern. “And it is not taken as a rule”: you may not make such words for other verbs; they are known from usage.
The pairs to remember: fāʿil and mafʿūl for the triliteral; mufʿil and mufʿal (one vowel apart) for every longer verb. The conjugation tool gives both for every sound pattern.

tasks.answer: Faʿīl, as qatīl, is turned from the origin mafʿūl; najan and nisy are used instead of mafʿūl; neither is a rule to apply to other verbs.

lessons.title: The maṣdar patterns of the triliteral
body: “The maṣdars have measures that I will set out”, and for the triliteral the poem gives a long list, four verses of pattern names. It begins with faʿl, fiʿl, fuʿl, then the same “with the tāʾ of the feminine or joined to the shortened alif”, then faʿlān, fiʿlān, fuʿlān. The poet's son Badr al-Dīn, in his commentary (Volck's edition), gives such examples as ḍarb, ʿilm, shughl, and layyān, ḥirmān, shukrān.

Then patterns named by example: jalan, riḍan, hudan and ṣalāḥ, that is faʿal, fiʿal, fuʿal and faʿāl. “Then add faʿil, bare or with the tāʾ”: kadhib and sariqa. Then faʿāla, and forms with the shortened alif and on faʿlāʾ; fiʿāla and fuʿāla, “and both bare of the tāʾ”; fuʿūl; faʿīl, and faʿīla and fuʿūla with the tāʾ; faʿalān; fayʿalūla, “like baynūna”; and fuʿul, “like shughul”.

The last two verses add the rarer ones: fuʿlal, faʿūl, faʿāliya, faʿīliyya, fuʿulla, faʿalā, faʿalūt, fuʿullā, fuʿalniya, fuʿūliyya (“and the fatḥa has been reported”: faʿūliyya too), and mafʿal, mafʿil, mafʿul, with and without the tāʾ, “and a ḍamma is rarely borne”. Badr al-Dīn's examples include sūdad for fuʿlal, qabūl for faʿūl, karāhiya for faʿāliya, ghulubba for fuʿulla and khuṣūṣiyya for fuʿūliyya.

The Marāḥ reports that Sībawayh counted thirty-two such patterns, and gives its own list of examples (its lesson 4); many of them illustrate the same patterns here, and the grid below takes its examples from there and from the poem.
These verses are a catalogue: they tell you that a word on such a pattern may be a maṣdar, not which maṣdar a verb has. The next lesson gives the rules for that.

lessons.title: Which maṣdar a triliteral verb takes
body: Now the rules (qiyās), where usage does not decide. “Faʿl is the rule for the transitive”: ḍaraba ḍarban, as the Marāḥ has it. “And fuʿūl for what is other than it”, the intransitive faʿala: dakhala dukhūlan. “Except a verb of sound: for this fuʿāl is plain”: an intransitive verb of crying or calling takes fuʿāl.

“And what is on faʿila, its maṣdar deserves, if it is not transitive, to be faʿal”: wajila wajalan, “he feared, a fearing”, from the Marāḥ. “And take faʿāla or fuʿūla as the rule for faʿula”: al-shajāʿa, “courage”, from shajuʿa, and the maṣdar of sahula, “it was easy”, suhūla.

“Whatever is other than that is heard”: a verb outside these rules has the maṣdar the Arabs gave it, learnt from usage. Then a set of patterns by meaning. Faʿīl “is frequent in sound”: verbs of noises (neighing, braying) often have it. “For the painful illness, the measure fuʿāl”, as names of ailments; “and for what has the sense of fleeing, or is like fleeing”, refusal, going away, fiʿāl, as firār, “flight”.

“Faʿāla is for qualities, and leave fiʿāla for a craft or an office”: faʿāla names a trait, fiʿāla a trade or a governing post. Badr al-Dīn's examples for these patterns elsewhere include ẓarāfa, “elegance”, and kitāba, “writing, the craft of the scribe”. Last, “for one time they set faʿla, and fiʿla for a manner, mostly, as mishyat al-khuyalā”, “the gait of the proud”: ḍarba, “one blow”, but mishya, “a way of walking”. The Marāḥ states the same pair: “faʿla for the single time, fiʿla for the manner”.
These rules give a good guess for an unknown verb; usage, where it is known, always wins.

tasks.prompt: What is the difference between faʿla and fiʿla? Use the poem's example.

lessons.title: The maṣdars of the longer verbs
body: The longer verbs have regular maṣdars, and the poem states them in a few rules. First the verbs with a hamza of joining: their maṣdar is made “with a kasra on the third letter” and “a lengthening of what the last follows”, a long ā before the last letter. Iḥtaqara gives iḥtiqār, inkasara inkisār, istakhraja istikhrāj: count the hamza as the first letter, and the third (the tāʾ, the kāf, the tāʾ) has the kasra.

“And give it a ḍamma in a verb to whose beginning the tāʾ is added”: the maṣdar of tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala is the past itself with a ḍamma on the letter before the last: tafaḍḍala, tafaḍḍul; taḍāraba, taḍārub. “And give it a kasra before a letter that admits weakness”: when the last root letter is weak, the ḍamma before it becomes a kasra.
“For faʿlala bring fiʿlāl and faʿlala”: zalzala, zilzāl, as the Marāḥ notes; daḥraja, daḥraja and diḥrāj, as the Maqṣūd recites it.

“And for faʿʿala make al-tafʿīl, where it is free of a weak lām”: qaṭṭaʿa, taqṭīʿ. “For the one that has it make tafʿila necessary”: a faʿʿala verb with a weak lām takes tafʿila, with the tāʾ, and never tafʿīl. “And to the one free of it, tafʿila has sometimes been given”: a sound faʿʿala verb may have tafʿila besides tafʿīl.
These rules are what the conjugation tool follows when it gives the maṣdar of an augmented pattern. For the triliteral, as the last lessons showed, it gives none: those maṣdars are learnt.

text.original:
بِكَسْرِ ثَالِثِ هَمْزِ الْوَصْلِ مَصْدَرُ فِعْ * لٍ حَازَهُ مَعَ مَدِّ مَا الْأَخِيرُ تَلَا
وَاضْمُمْهُ مِنْ فِعْلٍ التَّا زِيدَ أَوَّلَهُ * وَاكْسِرْهُ سَابِقَ حَرْفٍ يَقْبَلُ الْعِلَلَا
text.en:
With a kasra on the third [letter] of [a verb with] the hamza of joining, the maṣdar of a verb / that has it [is made], with a lengthening of what the last follows;
and give it a ḍamma in a verb to whose beginning the tāʾ is added, / and give it a kasra before a letter that admits weakness.

text.original:
لِفَعْلَلَ ائْتِ بِفِعْلَالٍ وَفَعْلَلَةٍ * وَفَعَّلَ اجْعَلْ لَهُ التَّفْعِيلَ حَيْثُ خَلَا
مِنْ لَامٍ اعْتَلَّ، لِلْحَاوِيهِ تَفْعِلَةً * أَلْزِمْ، وَلِلْعَارِ مِنْهُ رُبَّمَا بُذِلَا
text.en:
For faʿlala bring fiʿlāl and faʿlala; / and for faʿʿala make al-tafʿīl, where it is free
of a weak lām; for the one that has it make tafʿila / necessary; and to the one free of it [tafʿila] has sometimes been given.

lessons.title: More maṣdars of the longer verbs, and the tāʾ of once
body: Some less common maṣdars are also correct, and the poem praises their user: “whoever joins tafaʿʿala with tifiʿʿāl, and faʿʿala with al-fiʿʿāl, praise him for what he did”. The Marāḥ gives tiḥimmāl from taḥammala and killām from kallama; the Qurʾān has wa-kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā kidhdhāban (78:28), kidhdhāb from kadhdhaba.

“And tafʿāl may be brought for faʿʿala, in the multiplying of an act, as tasyār”, “much travelling”. The Marāḥ lists al-tahdār and al-talʿāb among the maṣdars of intensity. And fiʿʿīlā is made “for the triliteral, for intensity”, as al-ḥiththīthā and al-dillīlā in the Marāḥ; it may also stand in for tafāʿul.

“With al-fuʿallīla they have made ifʿalalla do without”, “not necessarily”: beside its regular maṣdar, ifʿalalla may take fuʿallīla, as Badr al-Dīn's commentary illustrates with qushaʿrīra, “shuddering”, and ṭumaʾnīna, “calm”. “For fāʿala make fiʿāl or mufāʿala”, as qātala, muqātala and qitāl; “and fiʿla has stood in for both”.

Then the tāʾ. In the hollow verb, ifʿāl and istifʿāl take a tāʾ “and compensation by it comes about for what was removed”: aqāma, iqāma; istaqāma, istiqāma. The dropped weak letter is made good by the tāʾ (the Marāḥ discusses the same tāʾ, and the iqāma of the Qurʾān without it).

Added to any other maṣdar, the tāʾ makes a noun of once: “a single time of the one who acted is made clear by it”. And when the maṣdar already has a tāʾ of its own, the single time “appears, for one who understands, by mentioning wāḥida”, “one”: you add the word “one” instead.

parts.title: Mafʿal and mafʿil, mafʿala and the instrument

lessons.title: Mafʿal and mafʿil: the rule and its exceptions
body: One pattern with a mīm serves for three things: the maṣdar (“the mīm maṣdar”), the place and the time. “From the triliteral that has no yafʿilu bring mafʿal”, both “for the maṣdar, or for what [the act] is done in”: where the muḍāriʿ has a fatḥa or a ḍamma, everything is mafʿal, as madhhab, madkhal, maqtal in the Marāḥ.

“Likewise what has a weak lām, absolutely”: marmā, from ramā yarmī, has a fatḥa even though its muḍāriʿ has a kasra. “And when the fāʾ is a wāw”, the noun “comes with a kasra, absolutely”: mawʿid, mawjil, even where the muḍāriʿ has a fatḥa (wajila yawjalu). But “the wāw's being the fāʾ has no effect when the lām is weak”, as mawlan: the weak lām's fatḥa wins (and the poet adds a pun on walāʾ, “so keep true friendship”).

“In other than this”, the verb with yafʿilu and a sound lām and no wāw: “give the ʿayn a fatḥa for a maṣdar, and in what is other than it a kasra”. So from jalasa yajlisu the place is al-majlis, with a kasra, as al-ʿIzzī has it, while its maṣdar with mīm takes the fatḥa. One vowel tells the maṣdar from the place. The Maqṣūd states the same rule, and names al-marjiʿ and al-maṣīr as maṣdars that came with a kasra all the same.

“And irregular is what departs from that”: a long list follows, maẓlama, maṭlaʿ, majmaʿ, maḥmada, madhamma, mansak, maḍanna, mazalla, mafraq, maḍalla, madabb, maḥshar, maskan, maḥall, maʿjaz, mahlaka, maʿtaba; mafʿal from waḍaʿa and wajila; mafʿala from ḥasiba and ḍaraba, and mawqaʿa. “All these have been given two ways”: they are heard with both vowels, against the rule. Our vowels follow Volck, who gives them with fatḥa; the commentary says each has both.

Compare the Marāḥ (its lesson 27): it gives the same rule from the future (mafʿal from yafʿalu, mafʿil from yafʿilu, the mithāl and the defective as exceptions) and its own list of nouns with kasra. The Lāmiyya adds the use for the maṣdar, and the words with both vowels.

tasks.prompt: Give the pattern of the maṣdar and of the place for: dhahaba yadhhabu; ramā yarmī; waʿada yaʿidu; jalasa yajlisu.
tasks.answer: Dhahaba: mafʿal for both (madhhab). Ramā: mafʿal for both, the lām being weak (marmā). Waʿada: mafʿil for both, the fāʾ being a wāw (mawʿid). Jalasa: mafʿal for the maṣdar, mafʿil for the place and time (al-majlis).

tasks.answer: Because its lām is weak too, and the poem says the wāw as fāʾ has no effect when the lām is weak: the weak lām's fatḥa wins.

tasks.prompt: What does the poem say of maẓlama, maṭlaʿ, majmaʿ and the rest of its list?
tasks.answer: That they depart from the rule (they are irregular), and that all of them are heard with two ways, fatḥa and kasra.

مِنْ ذِي الثَّلَاثَةِ لَا يَفْعِلْ لَهُ ائْتِ بِمَفْ * عَلٍ لِمَصْدَرٍ اوْ مَا فِيهِ قَدْ عُمِلَا
كَذَاكَ مُعْتَلُّ لَامٍ مُطْلَقًا، وَإِذَا الْ * فَا كَانَ وَاوًا بِكَسْرٍ مُطْلَقًا حَصَلَا
text.en:
From the triliteral that has no yafʿilu bring mafʿal / for the maṣdar, or for what [the act] is done in;
likewise what has a weak lām, absolutely; and when the / fāʾ is a wāw, [the noun] comes with a kasra, absolutely.

وَلَا يُؤَثِّرُ كَوْنُ الْوَاوِ فَاءً اذَا * مَا اعْتَلَّ لَامٌ كَمَوْلًى، فَارْعَ صِدْقَ وِلَا
فِي غَيْرِ ذَا عَيْنَهُ افْتَحْ مَصْدَرًا، وَسِوَا * هُ اكْسِرْ، وَشَذَّ الَّذِي عَنْ ذَلِكَ اعْتَزَلَا
text.en:
The wāw's being the fāʾ has no effect when / the lām is weak, as mawlan “master”: so keep true friendship.
In other than this give the ʿayn a fatḥa for a maṣdar, and in what is other / than it a kasra; and irregular is what departs from that:

مَزَلَّةٌ مَفْرَقٌ مَضَلَّةٌ وَمَدَبْ * بٌ مَحْشَرٌ مَسْكَنٌ مَحَلُّ مَنْ نَزَلَا

maẓlamatun “wrong done”, maṭlaʿu “rising”, al-majmaʿu “the gathering”, maḥmadatun “praise”, / madhammatun “blame”, mansakun “rite”, maḍannatu al-bukhalā “the miserliness of the misers”,
mazallatun “slipping”, mafraqun “parting”, maḍallatun “going astray” and madabb / “creeping”, maḥsharun “gathering”, maskanun “dwelling”, maḥallu man nazalā “the stopping-place of one who stopped”,

وَمَعْجَزٌ، وَبِتَاءٍ، ثُمَّ مَهْلَكَةٌ * مَعْتَبَةٌ، مَفْعَلٌ مِنْ ضَعْ وَمِنْ وَجِلَا
مَعْهَا مِنِ احْسِبْ وَضَرْبٍ وَزْنُ مَفْعَلَةٍ * مَوْقَعَةٌ، كُلُّ ذَا وَجْهَانِ قَدْ حُمِلَا

and maʿjazun “inability”, also with a tāʾ; then mahlakatun “destruction”, / maʿtabatun “reproach”; mafʿal from ḍaʿ “put!” and from wajilā “he feared”,
and with it, from iḥsib “suppose!” and from ḍarbin “hitting”, the measure mafʿala, / [as] mawqaʿatun “falling”: all these have been given two ways.

lessons.title: Words with kasra alone, and the other verbs
body: “Keep the kasra alone” in another set: marfiq, “elbow”, maʿṣiya, “disobedience”, masjid, “mosque”, makbir, “old age”, and maʾwin, the shelter “that holds the camels”. Then the mafʿila words from the verbs the verse names by their commands: from ighfir, maghfira, “forgiveness”; from iʿrif, maʿrifa, “knowledge”; from ʿudhr, iḥmi, razā and uẓnun the like; and manbit, “place of growth”.

“And join with mafʿil” the nouns from ushruq, ughrub, usquṭ, rajaʿa and ijzur, “rise, set, fall, return, slaughter”: mashriq, maghrib, masqiṭ, marjiʿ, majzir. Several of these are among the eleven nouns with kasra the Marāḥ lists from verbs with ḍamma in the future. Then mafʿila from iqdir, ushruq and uqbur, and from arib, and one of them takes all three vowels (the verse says “its fourth”; our reading of the end of that line is doubtful). “Likewise to mahlik the three vowels have been given”: mahlak, mahlik and mahluk, “destruction”.

“Like the sound is the one whose ʿayn is yāʾ”: a hollow verb with yāʾ follows the rule of the sound verb, mafʿal for the maṣdar and mafʿil for the place, as mabīʿ, “place of selling”, in the Marāḥ. “And on an opinion pause”: some hold otherwise; “do not go beyond what has been reported”.

Last, the longer verbs: “like the passive participle of what is not triliteral form from it” the noun of place, time or maṣdar. From istakhraja, mustakhraj is “extracted”, and also “a place, a time, or an act of extracting”.
The lists of these verses are learnt as they stand, like the doubled verbs of lesson 4. The rule behind them is simple; the words with kasra are the usage that departs from it.

lessons.title: The land of abundance, and the noun of instrument
body: A short section on a special noun: “from the noun of what is abundant, the name of the land is mafʿala, like masbaʿa”, “a land of many lions”, from sabuʿ, “lion”. The pattern is made from a noun, not from a verb: it names a place where that thing is found in plenty.

From a noun with an added letter, “the added is cut off”, as mafʿāt, “a land of many vipers”, from afʿā, “viper”, whose hamza is added. “And mufʿila and afʿalat have been allowed by them in this”: a land may also be called mufʿila, and one may say of it afʿalat, “it became full of …”. Badr al-Dīn illustrates these with muḍibba, “a land of many lizards”, and muqthiʾa, “a land of many cucumbers”.
“Other than the triliteral is barred from this pattern”: a noun of four root letters does not make a mafʿala; “and sometimes a rare one has come and been accepted”.

The last section, on the instrument: “like mifʿal, and like mifʿāl and mifʿala, from the triliteral form the name of what [the act] is done with”: the Marāḥ's miqrāḍ, “scissors”, and miftāḥ, “key”. “Irregular are al-muduqq”, the pestle, musʿuṭ, mukḥula, mudhun, munṣul, and the one from nakhala, the sieve (our reading of that last word is doubtful): instruments with a ḍamma.

“And whoever means [by them] an instrument may give them a kasra, and no heed is paid to one who blames him.” The Marāḥ reports Sībawayh on the same words: they are names of vessels, not instruments by the rule. So the two books agree: said with a ḍamma they are fixed names; made as instruments, they take the instrument's kasra.

lessons.title: The close, and the poem as a whole
body: “I have fulfilled what I aimed at, reaching the end; and praise be to God, since what I aimed at is complete.” The close answers the opening: praise of God, then blessing and peace “upon the noble Messenger, the seal of the messengers”, upon “his radiant family and his noble companions”, and upon whoever followed them “on the path of noble deeds”.

Then two prayers. One is for “a fair covering that wraps the slips”, the scholar's request that God cover the mistakes in his work: a modesty found at the end of many such poems. The other is for an effort by which he will be “rejoicing and glad, not frowning and afraid”. The last word, jadhilā, “glad”, ends the poem on its rhyme in lām.

Look back at the plan. The poem moves from the verb to the nouns made from it: the bare patterns and the vowel of their muḍāriʿ, the augmented patterns, the muḍāriʿ, the passive and the command; then the participles, the maṣdars, the nouns of time and place, the land of abundance and the instrument. The Marāḥ is ordered by the kind of root (sound, doubled, hamzated, weak); the Lāmiyya by the kind of form. Read together, they answer the two questions of ṣarf: what are the patterns, and what does each root do in them.
In our print the Lāmiyya is followed directly by Matn al-Sullam, al-Akhḍarī's poem on logic, taught on The Mantiqi: the same volume gathered the much-used mutūn of several sciences.
What remains is what the opening promised: “he may grasp the details who keeps the summaries in mind”. Learn the verses by heart; the details will come with every text you read.

tasks.prompt: What two things does the poet ask of God in the close?
tasks.answer: A fair covering that wraps his slips (that his mistakes be covered), and an effort by which he will be rejoicing and glad, not frowning and afraid.

tasks.prompt: Give the order of the poem's chapters.
tasks.answer: The bare verb and the vowel of its muḍāriʿ (with the hollow verb before -tu); the augmented verb; the muḍāriʿ; the passive; the command; the participles; the maṣdars of the triliteral and of the longer verbs; mafʿal and mafʿil; the land of abundance; the instrument; and the close.

tasks.prompt: How do the Lāmiyya and the Marāḥ differ in their order?
tasks.answer: The Marāḥ is ordered by the kind of root (sound, doubled, hamzated, mithāl, hollow, defective, lafīf), each taken through all its forms; the Lāmiyya is ordered by the kind of form (patterns, muḍāriʿ, passive, command, participles, maṣdars, nouns of place, instrument).
